title: Interior Design Introduction
summary: Learn the basics of interior design: the design process, elements and principles, space planning and measuring, colour, finishes and estimating paint and tiles, lighting and lux levels, and budgets, sustainability and careers. Calculations were checked in code.
audience: Homeowners, aspiring designers and decorators, property managers and small business owners

body.p: Interior design plans indoor spaces so they work well, feel good and reflect the people who use them. It goes beyond decoration: designers consider how people move, sit, work and rest, as well as light, air, safety, accessibility and budget. Good interiors improve comfort, productivity, health and the value of a property.

list: Homes: living rooms, kitchens, bedrooms and bathrooms.
Workplaces: offices, shops, salons and restaurants, where design supports the business and brand.
Hospitality: hotels, lodges and guesthouses.
Public spaces: schools, clinics, churches and community halls.

steps: Brief: understand the client's needs, lifestyle, style and budget.
Survey: measure and photograph the space.
Concept: mood boards and initial layouts.
Design development: furniture plans, finishes, lighting and costs.
Implementation: ordering, managing tradespeople and installation.

body.tip: Ask clients what they dislike about their current space; it often reveals their real needs faster than asking what they like.

list: Space: the area to be designed; positive space holds furniture, negative space is left open.
Line: horizontal lines feel calm and wide; vertical lines add height; curved lines soften.
Form and shape: the outlines and volumes of furniture and objects.
Light: natural and artificial, affecting mood and how colours look.
Colour: sets the atmosphere of a room.
Texture: rough wood, smooth tile, woven baskets and soft fabrics add depth.
Pattern: from tiles to textiles such as mudcloth or kitenge.

body.p: Balance (symmetrical, asymmetrical or radial), proportion and scale (furniture sized to the room and to each other), rhythm (repetition of colours or shapes), emphasis (a focal point such as an artwork or feature wall) and harmony (everything working as a whole) guide how elements are combined.

body.tip: Every room needs one clear focal point; too many competing features make a space feel chaotic.

body.p: Start with an accurate measured plan. A room 4 m by 3.5 m has a floor area of 14 m² and a perimeter of 2 x (4 + 3.5) = 15 m. Mark doors (and which way they swing), windows, sockets, switches and fixed features.

list: Leave walkways of about 900 mm where people pass; less feels cramped.
Allow around 450 mm between a sofa and a coffee table.
Plan for the work triangle in kitchens, linking sink, stove and fridge for efficient cooking.
Place furniture to encourage conversation, typically facing each other, not all against walls.
Design for accessibility: wider doorways, clear routes, lever handles and good lighting help older people and wheelchair users.

body.p: In open-plan spaces, create zones for cooking, eating, relaxing and working using rugs, lighting, furniture placement and changes of material, rather than walls.

body.tip: Make paper cut-outs of furniture to scale and move them on your plan before buying anything.

list: Warm colours (reds, oranges, yellows) feel energising and cosy; cool colours (blues, greens) feel calm and spacious.
Light colours make small rooms feel larger; dark colours make large rooms feel intimate.
A common guide is 60-30-10: 60% main colour, 30% secondary, 10% accent.
Test paint samples on the wall and view them in daylight and at night.

body.p: For the 4 m x 3.5 m room with 2.7 m high walls, the wall area is 15 x 2.7 = 40.5 m². Subtracting about 3.5 m² for a door and window leaves 37 m². Two coats at a coverage of 10 m² per litre need 37 x 2 / 10 = 7.4 litres.

Choose finishes for durability, cleaning and climate: tiles and polished concrete stay cool in hot regions; locally made furniture, woven grass, clay, reclaimed timber and textiles support local artisans and reduce transport costs. When ordering flooring, add about 10%: 14 m² of floor needs about 15.4 m² of tiles.

body.tip: Choose hard-wearing finishes for kitchens, entrances and children's rooms; save delicate materials for low-traffic areas.

list: Ambient lighting: general light for the whole room, such as ceiling lights.
Task lighting: focused light for activities such as reading, cooking or make-up.
Accent lighting: highlights artwork, plants or texture.
Natural light: maximise it with light colours, mirrors and uncluttered windows, while controlling glare and heat with blinds, overhangs and curtains.

body.p: Light levels are measured in lux (lumens per square metre). A living room might need about 150 lux: 150 x 14 m² = 2100 lumens. A study or kitchen work area might need about 300 lux: 300 x 14 = 4200 lumens, roughly 5.25 bulbs of 800 lumens each, so six bulbs or a combination of fixtures.

LED bulbs use far less electricity and last longer. Colour temperature matters: warm white (around 2700 to 3000 K) feels relaxing for living spaces; cool white suits work areas. Plan lighting with backup power and solar options where outages are common.

body.tip: Use several light sources at different heights instead of one bright ceiling light; rooms feel warmer and more flexible.

body.p: List every item with quantities and prices: for example furniture R2500, flooring R4000 and lighting R1500, a total of R8000. Add a contingency of about 10% (R800) for surprises. Prioritise items that are hard to change later, such as flooring and electrical points, then add decor over time.

list: Reuse and upcycle: reupholster or repaint existing furniture.
Buy from local makers and markets.
Choose low-VOC paints for healthier air.
Design for ventilation and passive cooling to reduce air-conditioning costs.

body.p: Interior designers and decorators work for design studios, architects, furniture retailers, property developers and hotels, or run their own businesses. Build a portfolio with before-and-after photos, learn tools such as SketchUp, and build a reliable network of carpenters, painters, electricians and suppliers.

body.tip: Put agreed designs, budgets and timelines in writing before work starts.
